draft.title: Properties of ionic compounds
card: An ionic compound is a lattice of positive and negative ions held together by strong electrostatic attraction. A lot of energy is needed to pull the ions apart.
High melting point
Ionic compounds are solid at room temperature and melt at high temperatures, because the strong attractions in the lattice must be overcome.
Brittle
A hard blow can shift one layer of ions so that ions of the same charge line up. They repel, and the crystal cracks or shatters.
Conduction
A solid does not conduct electricity, because its ions are fixed in place. When molten or dissolved in water, the ions are free to move and carry charge.
draft.remember: Strong attractions in the lattice give high melting points. Conduction needs ions free to move.

a.q: Why does solid sodium chloride not conduct electricity, while molten sodium chloride does?
opts: Its ions are fixed in solid, but free to move when molten
It has no ions in solid, but forms ions when it melts
Its electrons are fixed in solid, but free when molten
Its ions are attracted in solid, but repel when molten
a.why: In the solid lattice the ions cannot move, so no charge is carried. When molten, the ions are free to move and carry charge. Sodium chloride already has ions as a solid, so it does not form them on melting.
a.clue: Think about what carries the charge, and whether it can move.

b.q: A hammer strikes a crystal of magnesium oxide and it shatters into pieces. What best explains this?
opts: Layers shift and like-charged ions line up and repel
Layers slide over each other while electrons hold them
The strong attractions between ions are weak when struck
Free electrons are pushed out of the lattice by the blow
b.why: A blow shifts a layer of ions so ions of the same charge sit side by side. They repel and the crystal splits. Layers do not slide smoothly, because there is no sea of electrons to hold them together as in a metal.
b.clue: What happens when ions of the same charge end up next to each other?

a.best: Its ions are fixed in solid, but free to move when molten

b.best: Layers shift and like-charged ions line up and repel

problems.detail: The clue ('What happens when ions of the same charge end up next to each other?') effectively gives the answer away, since only one option mentions like-charged ions.
